title: Text, Characters, Unicode, and Encoding Basics
learningObjectives: Distinguish text, characters, and encoded byte representations at a basic level.
Explain why character encoding is needed to store and transmit text.
Describe Unicode as a standard for representing characters across writing systems.
Recognize that visible characters may involve multiple code points or bytes.
Identify common encoding problems such as corrupted text and incorrect assumptions about character length.

understand.concept: Text is a sequence of symbols used to communicate. A character is a unit of text, but what a user sees as one character may be represented by multiple code points or bytes. Unicode assigns code points to characters and related symbols across writing systems; encodings such as UTF-8 map those code points to bytes for storage or transmission.
understand.whyItMatters: Software must handle names, messages, symbols, multilingual input, and files reliably. Treating text as if every character were one byte or one fixed-width unit can break searching, display, slicing, validation, and data exchange.
understand.analogy: Unicode is like a large catalog assigning identifiers to symbols; an encoding is a method for packing those identifiers into a sequence of bytes for transport or storage.
understand.analogyLimit: Unicode and UTF-8 are related but not the same thing. A code point is not necessarily one byte or one visible character, and grapheme clusters can combine multiple code points.

explain.narrative: Text values are not simply a row of interchangeable numeric bytes. Unicode helps identify characters and symbols consistently, while an encoding defines how those identifiers become bytes. UTF-8 is widely used and can use different byte lengths for different code points. A visible character such as a letter with a combining mark, or an emoji sequence, may consist of multiple code points. When text appears as replacement symbols or mojibake, investigate decoding and encoding assumptions instead of deleting characters blindly.

examples.explanation: The byte sequence depends on the encoding, while the decoded text is what the reader sees.

examples.title: A symbol may take multiple bytes
examples.explanation: The euro symbol is a Unicode character and takes multiple bytes in UTF-8, unlike basic ASCII characters.

examples.title: Visible glyph vs code points
examples.code: const sample = 'é'; // e plus combining acute accent
examples.explanation: This may look like one accented character but can contain two Unicode code points; visual character counting requires grapheme-aware handling.

commonMistakes: Assuming one visible character always equals one byte.
Confusing Unicode code points with UTF-8 bytes.
Treating encoding and decoding as interchangeable without checking direction.
Assuming string length always equals the number of user-perceived characters.
Ignoring normalization or combining marks when comparing or counting text.
